query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy, intentionally enhanced nanoscale chemical heterogeneity (i.e. local compositional fluctuations resulting in nanoclusters) degrades toughness by locally impeding dislocation mobility and acting as weak links for crack initiation, independent of conventional grain‐boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a uniform elemental distribution and without significant grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Alter the processing conditions: one batch is subjected to extended high-temperature annealing to minimize local clustering (homogenized state), whereas a second batch is processed via rapid quenching or controlled thermal gradient treatments designed to promote nanoscale chemical heterogeneity.
generation.conditions: Mechanical loading tests conducted under service-relevant regimes (including conditions that provoke high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement) where maintaining the single-phase and compositionally complex nature is required.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized nanoclusters formed by compositional fluctuations within the matrix that serve as sites for reduced dislocation mobility and stress concentration.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced nanoscale chemical heterogeneity disrupts uniform plastic deformation by creating localized regions that preferentially nucleate brittle cracks. These nanoclusters diminish the material’s ability to redistribute stress during deformation, thereby lowering the ductile-to-brittle transition threshold compared to a homogenized alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical service conditions, HEA samples with induced nanoscale heterogeneity will exhibit an earlier onset of brittle fracture (evidenced by lower ductility and reduced toughness) compared to homogenized samples. In situ characterizations (e.g., high-resolution TEM or atom probe tomography) will reveal a correlation between the presence of nanoclusters and localized crack initiation sites.
generation.baseline: Homogenized HEA produced by extended high-temperature annealing, ensuring minimized local clustering, which is anticipated to retain superior ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to service and loading conditions where the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and the effects of conventional grain-boundary segregation are negligible; it is limited to regimes where processing history primarily affects nanoscale chemical fluctuations.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative threshold and spatial distribution of nanoscale heterogeneity required to trigger brittle behavior is not precisely defined, and other subtle microstructural changes might also influence toughness degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples: one set is homogenized via extended high-temperature annealing to minimize nanoscale chemical heterogeneity, and the other set is processed by rapid quenching or imposing localized thermal gradients to enhance nanoscale clustering. Subject both sets to identical mechanical loading tests under controlled conditions that mimic service environments (spanning both high temperature and low temperature regimes). Simultaneously, use in situ high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM) and atom probe tomography to monitor nanoscale compositional states, and record the onset strain for brittle fracture, ductility, and toughness.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of nanoscale chemical clustering via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM
Mechanical properties such as strain-to-failure, toughness, and ductility under controlled loading
Crack initiation and propagation behavior via real-time imaging techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples with intentionally enhanced nanoscale heterogeneity do not show a statistically significant earlier onset of brittle fracture or reduced ductility and toughness compared to the homogenized baseline, and if no correlation is found between the degree of nanoscale clustering and the fracture behavior, then the hypothesis that nanoscale clustering drives brittleness in these alloys will be falsified.

frame.system: A compositionally complex, initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) engineered for demanding service conditions.
frame.goal: To identify and test the mechanistic origins of toughness degradation (i.e. the emergence of brittle behavior) in these HEAs under service-relevant loading and environmental regimes.
frame.limitation: The current understanding does not explain why and how an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex alloy—without conventional grain-boundary segregation or obvious intermetallic precipitation—can suffer a loss of toughness.
root_cause_cues: grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation (in conventional alloys)
constraints: retain a compositionally complex alloy formulation
achieve performance suitable for demanding engineering service
frame.regime: Service conditions that include high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement; controlled mechanical loading tests designed to capture the transition from ductile to brittle behavior.
prior_attempts: Conventional alloy studies where toughness loss is attributed to grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation
Efforts that assumed similar mechanisms in HEAs without accounting for their intrinsic suppression of rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation
frame.understanding: A viable mechanistic hypothesis is that in high-entropy alloys, local compositional fluctuations and the emergence of short-range order (or nanoscale chemical heterogeneity) lead to the formation of localized ‘clusters’ that act as weak links during deformation. Unlike conventional alloys, where brittle behavior stems primarily from continuous grain-boundary phases or segregated intermetallics, in HEAs the nucleation of brittle behavior may be initiated by these localized chemical fluctuations that alter dislocation mobility and stress redistribution. A decisive experiment would involve a controlled comparison between two otherwise identical HEA states: one processed to minimize local solute clustering (via, for example, homogenization heat treatments) and another intentionally processed to promote subtle nanoscale chemical heterogeneity (e.g., via rapid quenching or localized thermal gradients). The hypothesis predicts that samples with promoted clustering will exhibit an earlier onset of brittle fracture under identical loading conditions compared to the homogenized baseline. Moreover, in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) and mechanical testing under service-like regimes should reveal differences in local deformation behavior. A falsification outcome would be if such controlled processing does not lead to any measurable differences in the fracture behavior, or if the presence or absence of local compositional heterogeneity does not correlate with the onset and propagation of brittle cracks—thereby supporting conventional expectations that only grain-boundary segregation governs toughness loss.

decision.trend: Early research on HEAs primarily assumed that toughness degradation would follow conventional alloy behavior such as grain‐boundary segregation or precipitate formation. However, continuing studies shifted the focus when high-resolution techniques (as in PMC6897545) revealed that even in single‐phase HEAs, nanoscale chemical fluctuations—nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries—can reduce cohesion and promote brittle crack nucleation. Although these insights implicate local compositional heterogeneity in ductility loss, the link between such nanoscale clustering and the emergence of brittle behavior in an otherwise homogeneous microstructure remains to be decisively proven.
decision.unsolved: It remains untested whether deliberately introduced nanoscale chemical fluctuations (short-range order or clustering) in a single-phase HEA are the primary drivers for premature brittle behavior, independent of conventional grain-boundary segregation. A controlled experiment that isolates the effect of local chemical heterogeneity on crack initiation and propagation under service-relevant loading is still missing.
decision.lever: Modulate processing conditions—compare a homogenized HEA (via extended high-temperature annealing to minimize local clustering) versus a rapidly quenched or thermally gradient‐processed HEA designed to promote subtle nanoscale chemical heterogeneity.
decision.why: This controlled comparison directly tests the hypothesis that local compositional fluctuations are responsible for weakening the alloy, as suggested by prior work. By keeping the overall single-phase and compositionally complex nature constant, any observed earlier onset of brittle fracture in the intentionally heterogeneous sample would affirm that nanoscale clustering, rather than conventional segregation, governs toughness degradation in these HEAs.
